title: List of qualifying R&D activities for software companies
description: Qualifying software R&D under IRC § 41 includes novel algorithms, AI models and architecture re-engineering that meet all four tests.
summary: Qualifying R&D activities for U.S. software companies under the federal research credit (IRC section 41) include novel algorithms and AI models, architecture re-engineering, and performance or security engineering, but each business component must meet all four tests, avoid the section 41(d)(4) exclusions, and, for internal-use software, pass the high threshold of innovation test.

body.text: Qualifying R&D activities for U.S. software companies under the federal research credit (IRC section 41) include novel algorithms and AI models, architecture re-engineering, and performance or security engineering, but each business component must meet all four tests, avoid the section 41(d)(4) exclusions, and, for internal-use software, pass the high threshold of innovation test.
It is general information, not tax or legal advice.
Summary

A software activity qualifies for the federal research credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 41 only when it meets all four statutory tests for each business component, is not caught by one of the section 41(d)(4) exclusions, and, if the software is developed primarily for internal use, also passes the high threshold of innovation test in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6).

The off-premises condition for computer-use costs is in the regulation itself, not only in the Form 6765 instructions. The quality-control exclusion and its “design of the product” carve-out sit in two different paragraphs of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2, and the citations have been made precise. The section 174A discussion now reflects the elective 60-month amortization option, the transition rules for unamortized 2022 through 2024 domestic costs, and the gross receipts test and timing of the small business retroactive election.
Legal framework for the list
Section 41 and the role of software

The research credit is codified at IRC § 41. A “business component” expressly includes computer software: the statute defines it as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business (IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)). Because the four-part test is applied to each business component separately, a software company's list of qualifying activities is, in practice, a list of business components (a product, a module, a feature set, or an internal process) together with the research activities performed on each one.
Interaction with sections 174 and 174A
Software development costs are treated as research or experimental expenditures by statute (IRC § 174(c)(3); now also IRC § 174A(d)(3)).

Correction. Section 174A was enacted by Pub. L. 119-21 (commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), title VII, § 70302(a), signed on July 4, 2025. Section 174A(a) allows a current deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. As an alternative, section 174A(c) lets a taxpayer elect to charge those expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months. Section 174 now applies only to foreign research or experimental expenditures, which remain amortized over 15 years. Section 41(d)(1)(A) now ties qualified research to expenditures treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A.

Transition rules. Pub. L. 119-21 gives taxpayers several options for domestic research costs that were capitalized under the prior rules in tax years beginning after December 31, 2021 and before January 1, 2025. Any taxpayer may elect to deduct the remaining unamortized amount in the first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over the two tax years beginning with that year. Eligible small business taxpayers (those that are not tax shelters and that meet the section 448(c) gross receipts test, an average of $31 million or less over the three prior tax years, for their first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024) may instead elect to apply section 174A retroactively to those earlier years. The IRS issued the procedures in Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (August 28, 2025), and the current Instructions for Form 6765 point taxpayers to that revenue procedure for the transition options. The amended-return route for the small business retroactive election was generally available only until July 6, 2026, so for most taxpayers that window has now closed; a taxpayer that missed it should confirm with an adviser which, if any, method-change route remains available.

The point that the activity-level qualification and documentation standards are unchanged remains accurate, since the four-part test in section 41(d) did not change. For a software company, this means the list of qualifying activities set out below governs both the credit and, through the cross-reference in section 41(d)(1)(A), the population of costs treated as domestic research expenditures.
The four-part test applied to software

All four tests must be met, and the IRS applies them separately to each business component. Failing any one disqualifies the activity. Where the tests are not met at the level of the whole business component, the regulations apply a “shrinking-back” rule that moves the analysis to the next most significant subset of elements, so a qualifying sub-project can still be claimed even if the larger product does not qualify as a whole.
Permitted purpose

Research must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Research related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors does not qualify (IRC § 41(d)(3)). The taxpayer does not have to succeed in developing the new or improved component for the research to qualify (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)). For software, this means that work aimed at measurable technical properties (speed, accuracy, scalability, fault tolerance, security) can meet the purpose test, while work aimed only at visual appearance cannot.
Elimination of technical uncertainty (section 174 test)

The costs must be research costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, meaning activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty about developing or improving a product. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)).
Correction. It is not the U.S. standard. Under U.S. regulations the test turns on the information available to the taxpayer, as stated above.
Process of experimentation

A process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain. It may involve modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)). The IRS audit techniques guide frames this as identifying the uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives, and conducting a process of evaluating them.

Correction. The rule is fixed by statute and regulation: “substantially all” of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation (IRC § 41(d)(1)), and substantially all means 80 percent or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)). The 80 percent figure is a floor, not a ceiling.
Technological in nature

Information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)). Research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities is excluded (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G)).

New or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality; not style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design (§ 41(d)(3))
Designing an authentication protocol with improved reliability and access control

Not knowing how to integrate third-party APIs while keeping latency under a set target
Process of experimentation

Technological in nature

Applying distributed-systems and network principles to meet performance targets

body.text: Categories of qualifying software activities

Each is qualifying only when the specific project meets the four tests above. Where the IRS has given a view, it is noted. The IRS “Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software” (page last reviewed June 8, 2026) group software activities by audit risk. Activities that rarely fail to constitute qualified research (low risk) are the initial release of an application software product that may require new constructs; the development of system software such as operating systems and compilers; the development of specialized technologies such as image processing, artificial intelligence, or speech recognition; and software developed as part of a hardware product where the software interacts directly with that hardware. The guidelines state that they are not an official pronouncement of the law and cannot be used, cited, or relied upon as such.
Novel algorithms and AI or machine learning models

This is consistent with the IRS's low-risk rating for artificial intelligence, image processing, and speech recognition work. [Analysis] Selecting among commercially available models or vendor tools is also unlikely to qualify on its own, since the IRS guidelines rate studies to select vendor products as high risk.
Software architecture and infrastructure

Caution added. The IRS software audit guidelines rate re-hosting or porting an application to a new hardware or software platform, software application configuration, and upgrading to newer versions of hardware or software or installing vendor fix releases as high-risk activities that usually fail to constitute qualified research. Changing from a product based on one technology to a product based on a different or newer technology is rated moderate risk. A cloud migration is therefore not qualifying in itself; only the portion involving a process of experimentation to resolve uncertainty can be claimed. [Analysis]
Cybersecurity, performance optimization, and system integration

These fit the permitted purposes of improved performance, reliability, or quality in § 41(d)(3). The IRS rates functional enhancements to existing applications as moderate risk, depending on the facts.

Caution added. The IRS guidelines list “interfaces” among high-risk activities. System integration work that connects existing systems through established interfaces is therefore unlikely to qualify unless the taxpayer can show genuine uncertainty about the capability, method, or design of the integration and a process of experimentation to resolve it. [Analysis]
Activities across the development lifecycle

items: Feasibility analysis to determine technical viability and the requirements needed to meet performance goals
Architecture and design work, including iterative revisions intended to resolve uncertainty about capability or design
Prototyping to test functionality and evaluate alternatives
Unit, integration, acceptance, and alpha or beta testing conducted as part of the process of experimentation

body.text: The regulations support the testing point within limits. Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) excludes the ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control, and § 1.174-2(a)(7) defines quality control testing to exclude testing to determine whether the design of the product is appropriate. [Analysis] The IRS guidelines also rate detecting flaws and bugs in software as high risk, so testing that only finds and fixes defects in an already-settled design should be kept out of a claim.
Illustrative qualifying and non-qualifying pairs (hypothetical)
These are illustrations, not IRS determinations.

A new sharding algorithm for data growth where standard database approaches fail
Database version updates, standard data migration, routine fixes of known bugs

A custom rendering engine to display millions of data points in real time in a browser
Rearranging widgets, changing color palettes (style or cosmetic factors excluded by § 41(d)(3))

A new neural network architecture where existing models are not accurate enough
Routine training of standard models without architectural change

A new encryption method for low-latency devices where standard protocols are too heavy
Connecting systems with standard REST APIs and documenting endpoints

body.text: Note added. The IRS guidelines rate graphical user interface work as high risk. The frontend example above is plausible only because the uncertainty lies in the rendering engine's performance (a computer-science problem), not in the interface's layout or appearance. The integration example in the non-qualifying column is consistent with the guidelines' high-risk rating for interfaces. [Analysis]
Internal-use software
Definition and what falls outside it

Research on software developed by or for the benefit of the taxpayer primarily for internal use is excluded unless regulations provide otherwise (IRC § 41(d)(4)(E)). Under the final regulations (T.D. 9786, published October 4, 2016, and applicable to tax years beginning on or after that date), internal-use software is software developed for use in general and administrative functions that facilitate or support the taxpayer's trade or business, limited to financial management, human resources management, and support services functions (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)). Software developed to be sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties is not internal-use software, nor is software developed to let the taxpayer interact with third parties or let third parties initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system.
Correction to citation. That release is dated January 16, 2015 and announced the proposed regulations. The rules in force are the final regulations in T.D. 9786.
High threshold of innovation test
Internal-use software qualifies only if it also meets all three parts of the test in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii):

items: Innovative: the software would result in a reduction in cost, improvement in speed, or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant, if development is successful.

Significant economic risk: the taxpayer commits substantial resources to development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period.
Not commercially available: the software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer.

body.text: [Analysis] For a software company, most product development is software held for sale, lease, or license or software that lets customers interact with the company's systems, so it falls outside the internal-use definition and needs only the four-part test. The high threshold of innovation test matters mainly for back-office tools (finance, HR, and support services systems) that the company builds for its own administrative use.
Excluded activities
Routine work and quality control

Excluded activities include routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control and routine data collection (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5)). The IRS audit techniques guide illustrates the arts exclusion: developing a new artist's paint formulation is not excluded because it benefits the arts, but research into an artist's life is. For software, the IRS audit guidelines identify maintenance of existing applications, software application configuration, installing vendor fix releases, detecting flaws and bugs, and data quality, data cleansing, and data consistency activities as high-risk activities that usually fail to constitute qualified research.
Adaptation, duplication, and reverse engineering

Research related to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need is excluded (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B)), but the IRS notes the exclusion does not apply merely because a component is intended for a specific customer. Research related to reproducing an existing business component, in whole or in part, from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information is excluded (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C)). This exclusion does not apply merely because the taxpayer evaluates another's business component. The IRS software audit guidelines list reverse engineering as a high-risk activity, and the IRS treats reverse engineering as outside qualified research under § 41(d).
Clarification. The statutory adaptation exclusion is narrower: it targets adaptation to a particular customer's requirement or need.
Foreign research and non-technical fields

Research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any U.S. possession is excluded (IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)). The IRS confirms this covers in-house and contract research, even if done by American researchers or for an American taxpayer. Research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities is excluded (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G)). [Analysis] For software companies with offshore development teams, work performed abroad cannot be included in the credit, and its costs are foreign research expenditures that remain subject to 15-year amortization under section 174.
Funded research

Research is excluded to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H)). The IRS audit techniques guide asks whether payment is contingent on the success of the research and whether the performer retains substantial rights in the results; if not, the research is treated as funded. For software companies performing development under fixed-price customer contracts, the contract terms on payment and intellectual property ownership decide whether the work can be claimed.
Qualified research expenses for software claims
Wages

Wages qualify for qualified services: engaging in qualified research, or the direct supervision or direct support of research activities that constitute qualified research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)). Direct supervision means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research and does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)). Direct support does not include general administrative services such as payroll or accounting (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)).
Contract research

Generally 65 percent of amounts paid to a non-employee for qualified research count as contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)(A)). Higher percentages apply in specific cases: 75 percent for qualified research consortia and 100 percent for certain energy research by eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories (Form 6765 instructions). The taxpayer must bear the cost even if the research is not successful: where payment is contingent on the success of the research, the contingent portion is treated as paid for the product or result rather than for the performance of the research and is not a contract research expense (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)). Prepaid amounts are treated as paid in the period in which the qualified research is conducted (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(4)).
Supplies and computer use, including cloud costs

The statute defines supplies as any tangible property other than land or improvements to land and property of a character subject to depreciation (IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)). Supplies that are indirect research expenditures, and general and administrative expenses, do not qualify (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1)).

Amounts paid to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research qualify (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)). The regulation itself contains all three conditions: the computer must be owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, must be located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer must not be the primary user of the computer (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4)).
Documentation and reporting
Form 6765 Section G

The requirement comes from the form and its instructions, not the statute, and its timing is phased. Under the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), finalized by the IRS in February 2026, Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025. For calendar-year taxpayers, the first return that must include Section G is the 2026 return, filed in 2027. A filer is not required to complete it if it is a qualified small business that checks the box to elect the payroll tax credit, or if its QREs (determined at the controlled group level) are $1.5 million or less, its average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less, and it reports the credit on an original return. Where required, Section G breaks out wages for direct research, direct supervision, and direct support, plus supplies, computer rental, and contract research, by business component.
Evidence from engineering systems

These are practice recommendations rather than legal requirements. They map onto the regulatory elements a claim must show: the uncertainty, the alternatives evaluated, and the 80 percent substantially-all measure. With Section G now required for most filers from the 2026 tax year, records organized by business component will also be needed to complete the form itself.
Context figures

The 2024 Research and Development Tax Credit Report to the Pennsylvania General Assembly (May 2024 awards for the 2023 application year) shows the Information sector received $8.2 million, 13.7 percent of $60.0 million in awards, and the largest award per recipient. Software publishers, internet tool providers, web hosting, and computer infrastructure firms received 75 percent of the Information sector's awards.
They are not used in this report.
